metadata.title: Deciphering socioeconomic inequality in science literacy: Evidence from PISA 2015 in Türkiye

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for Türkiye, targeting 15-year-old students enrolled at least from grade 7. The analytic sample is drawn via PISA’s stratified random sampling across 187 schools, with most students in grade 10 and the remainder largely in grade 9. For estimation, the authors explicitly apply the PISA student-level sampling weight W_FSTUWT within HLM 7 and also rely on IDB Analyzer-generated SPSS syntax that accounts for weighting in the regression analyses. The paper does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), but it does state that weights are used to better represent the target population.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper describes that science literacy is estimated using 10 plausible values and that HLM 7 and IDB Analyzer analyze each plausible value separately and combine results appropriately. However, it does not explicitly document a missing-data strategy for questionnaire/background variables (e.g., whether missing covariates were imputed or cases were excluded). This is a reporting gap because PISA datasets typically contain missingness in contextual variables, and the choice of deletion vs. imputation can affect regression coefficients and variance explained.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 Türkiye data for 15-year-old students attending at least grade 7. The sample is the PISA 2015 stratified random sample for Türkiye (5895 selected students from 187 schools), with the reported analytic N in the results tables being 5859 students for the SES–science literacy descriptive/correlation analyses. No additional task-level or variable-level exclusions are described beyond the use of the PISA science literacy plausible values and the available SES sub-dimension variables.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Türkiye (15-year-olds, Science literacy major domain; plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Correlation SES–science literacy: r=0.30 (p<.001). HLM unconditional model: ICC=0.551 (p<.001). HLM student-level SES effect: B=1.33, p=.129 (within-school variance explained L1 R2=0.005). HLM school-level SES effect: B=56.43, p<.001 (between-school variance explained L2 R2=0.494).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Türkiye the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS) alongside school-type and regional stratification to explain science literacy, finding that ESCS did not significantly predict science literacy at the student level (B=1.33, p=.129) but strongly predicted differences between schools (B=56.43, p<.001; L2 R2=0.494). This indicates that educational inequality in science literacy in Türkiye is primarily structured through between-school SES sorting (tracking), implying that equity policies should prioritize school-level resource and placement mechanisms rather than only targeting individual student SES.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Türkiye (15-year-olds, Science literacy major domain; HLM by school type)
main_findings.target_variable: Science literacy (PISA 2015 plausible values) — school-type differences
main_findings.performance_metrics: School-type descriptive differences: General Secondary Education vs Vocational & Technical Secondary Education: Cohen’s d=0.96 for science literacy. HLM school-level SES explained variance: General Secondary Education L2 R2=0.504; Vocational & Technical Secondary Education L2 R2=0.188. Student-level SES effects by school type: General Secondary Education B=2.87, p=.020 (L1 R2=0.008); Vocational & Technical Secondary Education B=-0.58, p=.677 (L1 R2=0.002).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Türkiye the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS) and school type to explain science literacy, finding that SES explained substantially more between-school variance in General Secondary Education (L2 R2=0.504) than in Vocational & Technical Secondary Education (L2 R2=0.188). This indicates that tracking into different secondary school pathways may amplify SES-linked science literacy inequality in specific school types, suggesting that reforms should target how students are assigned and supported within those pathways.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Türkiye (15-year-olds, Science literacy major domain; HLM by statistical region)
main_findings.target_variable: Science literacy (PISA 2015 plausible values) — SES–science literacy relationship by region
main_findings.performance_metrics: Regional descriptive differences: West Marmara (TR02) vs Middle East Anatolia (TR11) science literacy mean difference corresponds to Cohen’s d=1.01 (447.6 vs 382.2). HLM school-level SES explained variance by region ranged from L2 R2=0.020 (TR11) to L2 R2=0.833 (TR02). Student-level SES effects were not statistically significant across regions (all reported p-values > .05 in Table 4).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Türkiye the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS) and statistical region to explain science literacy, finding that the SES–science literacy relationship varies strongly by region at the school level (L2 R2 from 0.020 in TR11 to 0.833 in TR02) while student-level SES effects remain non-significant. This indicates that regional education inequality mechanisms operate through school contexts, implying that regional targeting of school improvement and resource allocation is necessary rather than applying a uniform national SES–science literacy intervention.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Türkiye (15-year-olds, Science literacy major domain; regression via IDB Analyzer)
main_findings.target_variable: Science literacy (PISA 2015 plausible values) — SES sub-dimensions
main_findings.performance_metrics: Regression R2 (variance explained): Mother’s occupational status BMMJ1 standardized=.36, R2=.13; Father’s occupational status BFMJ2 standardized=.27, R2=.07; Highest parental occupational status HISEI standardized=.29, R2=.08. Educational level: MISCED R2=.01; FISCED R2=.03; HISCED R2=.03; PARED R2=.03. Home possessions: HOMEPOS standardized=.33, R2=.11; WEALTH standardized=.29, R2=.09; HEDRES standardized=.25, R2=.06; CULTPOSS standardized=.21, R2=.04; ICTRES standardized=.33, R2=.11.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Türkiye the study leveraged SES sub-dimensions to predict science literacy, finding that occupational status and home possessions explain more variance than parental education level (e.g., ICT resources R2=.11 and mother occupational status R2=.13 vs. educational level components R2≈.01–.03). This indicates that policies aiming to reduce science literacy inequality in Türkiye should prioritize economic/social capital supports (e.g., access to ICT and learning resources, and support linked to parental occupational advantages) rather than focusing primarily on parental education.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2015 Türkiye microdata for 15-year-olds (science literacy as the major domain) and estimates science literacy using 10 plausible values, combining results across plausible values via HLM 7 and IDB Analyzer. The analytic sample reported in the results tables is N=5859 students from 187 schools, with student sampling weights applied (W_FSTUWT). Using a two-level hierarchical linear model (students nested within schools), the authors find a moderate SES–science literacy correlation (r=0.30, p<.001) but a non-significant student-level SES effect (B=1.33, p=.129) alongside a strong school-level SES effect (B=56.43, p<.001; L2 R2=0.494; ICC=0.551). SES–science literacy relationships vary by region at the school level (L2 R2 up to 0.833 in TR02), and SES sub-dimensions show that occupational status and home possessions (including ICT resources) explain more variance than parental education. Limitations include the correlational, cross-sectional design and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling for contextual covariates.
